blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: In the beer lesson, we visited three cities in Germany and drank their beer. Today we eat there. We will learn the famous dishes, the stories behind their names and the best beer for each.

items.prompt: What food do you like to eat with beer?
Have you ever eaten German food? What was it like?
What do you want to eat on a cold winter day?

blocks.title: Part 1: Funny Food Names in Cologne
paragraphs: Almost every menu in a Cologne brewery pub has a dish called **Halve Hahn**. In the **dialect** of Cologne, the local way of speaking, the name says *half a rooster*. A **rooster** is a male chicken. **But when your plate arrives, there is no chicken on it.**

**A Halve Hahn is half of a Röggelchen, a small, dark rye roll.** You met this roll in the beer lesson. Bakers put the rolls in the oven in pairs, so two rolls touch and bake together. Later they break them apart. On your half you get butter, a thick slice of Gouda, strong **mustard** and rings of raw onion. Gouda is a yellow cheese from the Netherlands. It is soft and a little salty.

So why the funny name? **Nobody knows for sure, and people in Cologne tell different stories.** The best-known story takes place at a birthday party in the late 1800s. As a joke, a man ordered half a rooster for each of his friends. He told the waiter his plan first. The friends waited for roast chicken, but the waiter brought rye rolls with cheese. Everyone laughed, and the joke became the name of the dish. It is a nice story, but nobody can say if it is true.

The Halve Hahn is a perfect partner for Kölsch, the light, pale beer of Cologne. The snack is simple and salty, and the mustard and raw onion are sharp. **A cold, light beer cleans your mouth after these strong tastes.** So you want another bite, and then another small glass.

The second funny name in Cologne is **Himmel un Ääd**, dialect for *heaven and earth*. **It is mashed potatoes mixed with cooked apples.** So it is soft, a little sweet and a little sour. With it you usually get fried **black pudding**, a dark sausage made with pig's blood. You also get fried onions.

**The name comes from where the food grows.** Apples grow high up in trees, near the sky. In German, Himmel is the word for both sky and heaven. Potatoes grow in the ground, in the earth. So one plate holds heaven and earth.

blocks.title: Part 2: Sauerbraten, a Sweet and Sour Roast
paragraphs: **Sauerbraten is the famous roast of the Rhineland.** This is the region along the river Rhine, where Cologne and Düsseldorf are. You find it in the brewery pubs of both cities. The name is German: sauer is sour, and Braten is roast meat.

**Before cooking, the beef is marinated: it lies in a liquid for three days or more.** This liquid, the **marinade**, is made of **vinegar**, wine and spices such as **bay leaves** and pepper. Then the cook takes the meat out and cooks it slowly for hours.

Why so much vinegar? Before people had fridges, meat went bad quickly. **Vinegar is sour and strong, and it helped meat stay fresh for longer.** It also makes hard meat softer. So a cook could buy a cheaper, harder piece of beef. After days in the marinade and hours of slow cooking, it is very soft. It falls apart under your fork.

In the Rhineland, the sauce is not only sour. Cooks add **raisins**, and sometimes **gingerbread** or **sugar-beet syrup**. Gingerbread is a sweet cake made with spices. The syrup is dark and thick, and it is made from sugar beets, a root used for sugar. **So the sauce becomes sweet and sour, dark and thick.**
On the plate you usually find **potato dumplings**, big soft balls made of potato. Next to them is **red cabbage**, cooked until it is soft and sweet. Some places also give you **apple sauce**.

There is one more thing to know. **In the Rhineland, Sauerbraten was traditionally made with horse meat.** Today most pubs use beef, because many guests do not want to eat horse. Only a few traditional places still make it with horse. So read the menu carefully: Pferd is German for horse. If the menu says Sauerbraten vom Pferd, the meat is horse.

images.alt: Slices of dark Sauerbraten in a thick brown sauce with raisins, with round potato dumplings and red cabbage on a white plate

items.prompt: Why did cooks leave the meat in vinegar for days?
items.answer: Vinegar kept meat fresh for longer before there were fridges, and it made hard meat soft.

blocks.title: Part 3: Mustard in Düsseldorf
paragraphs: **In Düsseldorf, the taste of the city is mustard.** Locals call it **Mostert**, an old local word for mustard. It is strong and spicy. If you eat too much at once, you feel it in your nose.

Mustard has been made in Düsseldorf since 1726. In that year, the first mustard factory in Germany opened in the city. The brand ABB says its story starts with that factory. Since 2012, Düsseldorfer Mostert has been a **protected name** in the European Union. **Only mustard made in Düsseldorf may use this name.** A company in another city can make mustard in the same way. But it cannot call it Düsseldorfer Mostert. Kölsch has a protected name too. In both cases, the name tells you where the product really comes from.

The other famous brand is Löwensenf: Löwe is lion, and Senf is mustard. **It did not start in Düsseldorf.** It began in 1903 in Metz, a city that was part of Germany at that time. After the First World War, Metz became part of France. So the company moved to Düsseldorf.

Düsseldorf also has a dish that shows off its mustard: **Düsseldorfer Senfrostbraten**. Here the Rostbraten is a rump steak, a thick slice of beef from near the cow's tail. The cook fries the steak and covers the top with Düsseldorf mustard and chopped onion. **The heat turns this top into a dark, spicy crust**, a hard top. People eat it with fried potatoes and Altbier, the dark beer of Düsseldorf.

Why does strong mustard go well with this beer? Altbier is dark and **malty**: it tastes a little like the dark crust of bread. At the end, it is a little bitter. **This round, bread-like taste calms the sharp mustard.** The bitter taste and the bubbles clean the fat from your mouth. The food is spicy and sharp, the beer is calm, and together they are in balance.

images.alt: A small stoneware pot of brown Düsseldorf mustard beside a thick beef steak with a dark crust of mustard and onion, fried potatoes and a glass of dark Altbier

items.prompt: Can a mustard company in Cologne sell its mustard as Düsseldorfer Mostert?
items.answer: No. Since 2012, only mustard made in Düsseldorf may use that name.

blocks.title: Part 4: A Pepper Stew in Dortmund
paragraphs: The famous dish of Dortmund has a long name: **Pfefferpotthast**. The name has three parts. Pfeffer is pepper, Pott is pot, and the last part is an old word for a piece of beef. **So the name tells you what it is: beef with pepper, cooked in a pot.**

**Pfefferpotthast is a beef stew: meat cooked slowly in liquid until it is very soft.** It is an old dish of Westphalia, the region around Dortmund. It was a meal for working people. The cook fries pieces of beef. Then the beef boils slowly in a pot for a long time, with lots of onions. Bay leaves and plenty of black pepper go in too. The onions almost melt and make the stew sweet, and the pepper makes it spicy.

The surprise is how the stew becomes thick. Most cooks use flour for this, but **Pfefferpotthast uses bread crumbs**. The crumbs take in the liquid and make the sauce thick. They also give it a deep bread taste. You eat it with boiled potatoes and **gherkins**, small sour cucumbers kept in vinegar. Between hot, heavy bites of stew, a cold, sour gherkin is a nice change.

The dish also has a **legend**, linked to Agnes von der Vierbecke and the year 1378. In the story, Agnes worked with enemies who wanted to take Dortmund. She asked the gatekeeper, the man at the city gate, to fetch her a pot of Pfefferpotthast from the market. While he was away, the gate had no guard. That was her plan. **It is only a legend: historians have little proof for it.** Dortmund celebrates the dish anyway. Every autumn, there is a Pfefferpotthast festival on the Alter Markt, the old market square.

To drink, choose a Dortmund Export. It is a golden beer, soft and round, with a light bitter taste at the end. Pepper burns your mouth, and the cold beer calms it. **In an Export, the sweet malt and the bitter taste are in balance.** So the beer does not fight with the spicy stew.

images.alt: A bowl of Pfefferpotthast, a dark beef stew with soft onions and black pepper, with boiled potatoes and sliced gherkins on the side

Part 5: Christmas Markets in December
paragraphs: **In December, the squares of all three cities fill with Christmas markets.** Small wooden huts sell hot wine, sweets, gifts and food.

**The favourite market food in Cologne is Reibekuchen: fried potato pancakes.** The cook grates raw potatoes and onions into tiny pieces. Then the cook presses out the water and adds egg, flour and salt. Spoons of this mix go into hot oil. They fry until they are brown, **crispy** at the edges and soft in the middle. You eat them hot, with apple sauce. In the Rhineland, people also eat them with Rübenkraut, the sugar-beet syrup from the Sauerbraten part. Hot, salty potato with something sweet is a popular mix here.

Why is so much market food hot and fried? December is cold, and people walk from hut to hut for hours. **Hot food warms you from inside and keeps you full.** A hot paper plate also warms cold hands. Frying is fast, too: a pancake is ready in a few minutes. So one stall can sell fresh food to a long line of people. And you can eat it with your hands, with no table.

The Christmas market in Dortmund has something huge. The city calls its tree the largest Christmas tree in the world. **It is about 45 metres tall, but it is not one tree.** For each market, workers build a tall frame and fix more than 1,000 small **spruce** trees on it. A spruce is a Christmas tree with short, sharp needles. From far away, all the small trees look like one giant tree. Dortmund has built it almost every year since 1996.

images.alt: Golden, crispy potato pancakes with apple sauce on a paper plate at a busy Christmas market in the evening, with wooden huts and lights behind

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: Christmas Markets in December

items.prompt: Why do Christmas markets sell so much hot, fried food?
items.answer: People walk outside in the cold for hours. Hot food warms them, and frying is fast.

blocks.title: Scene: Ordering in a Cologne Brewery Pub
paragraphs: It is a cold December evening. You sit down in a busy brewery pub in Cologne. The waiter, a Köbes in a blue apron, comes over with glasses of Kölsch.
Your goal: find out what Halve Hahn is and order it with a Kölsch. Then ask if the Sauerbraten is beef or horse.

blocks.title: Conversation: Ordering in a Cologne Brewery Pub

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, please. And what is Halve Hahn? Is it chicken?

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: No chicken at all. It's half a rye roll with butter, a thick slice of Gouda, mustard and raw onion.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: So the name is a joke! How much is it?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'd like a Halve Hahn, please. Is the mustard very strong?

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: Yes, it's quite strong. That's why it goes so well with a cold Kölsch.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. And the Sauerbraten: is it beef or horse?

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: Ours is beef. Only a few pubs in Cologne still make it with horse. In those pubs, the menu says Pferd.

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: Potato dumplings and red cabbage. Apple sauce too, if you want it. It's 22.50 euros.

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: Sweet and sour. The sauce has raisins in it.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Then I'll have the Sauerbraten too, after the Halve Hahn.

turns.speaker: Köbes
turns.text: Good choice. Here's your Kölsch. Cheers!

paragraphs: In pairs, one of you is a Köbes in a Cologne pub, and the other orders food and a Kölsch.
